steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a programming languages paper introducing Outcome Separation Logic, a program logic with a frame rule that works for both correctness and incorrectness reasoning in programs with effects. Explain the motivation from static analysis and bug finding, what existing separation logics can't handle, our contributions (the logic and symbolic execution algorithms), and give a roadmap of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Compositional reasoning and static analysis at scale
- Verification vs. bug finding; Incorrectness Logic and ISL
- Why no existing logic's frame rule covers effects, may/must properties and under-approximation
- Our contribution: Outcome Separation Logic
- Our contribution: symbolic execution algorithms, bi-abduction and tri-abduction
- Paper outline

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Compositional reasoning at scale
  - separation logic (cite) + bi-abduction (cite)
  - static analysis scaled to industrial software, hundreds of millions of lines of code
  - analyze code changes w/o disrupting fast-paced engineering culture (cite)
- Verification vs. bug finding
  - fully automated verification elusive; tools still boost confidence: program won't go wrong in many ways
  - C/C++: no segmentation fault crash, no memory leak
  - failure to prove absence of bugs != incorrect program; could be false positive
  - many programs are incorrect; bug-finding tools sometimes more useful, errors -> tangible code improvements (cite)
  - motivated by this: Incorrectness Logic (cite), Incorrectness Separation Logic (ISL) (cite), recently
- Limits of existing logics
  - ISL compositional like SL, but SL and ISL semantics incompatible; specs and tools can't be shared
  - soundness of local reasoning relies on particular assumptions; no single logic with a frame rule for all of:
  - Computational Effects: commands must be local actions (cite), central to frame rule; allocation semantics forced nondeterministic (cite); unsuitable for e.g. probabilistic computation
  - May and Must properties: SL only must, ISL only may; need both
  - Under-approximation: bug finding inspects subset of paths (those leading to a bug); many SLs fault avoiding -> precondition covers all traces, whole program inspected; unsuitable for incorrectness
- Outcome Separation Logic (OSL)
  - local reasoning sound under new assumptions; no particular evaluation model forced; fits correctness + incorrectness
  - extension of Outcome Logic (OL) (cite) to pointer programs; OL: correctness + incorrectness, variety of effects; metatheory, inference rules carry over
  - key novelty: separation-logic-style heap assertions -> frame rule, compositional symbolic execution
  - hard: frame rule soundness intricate even in partial correctness Hoare Logic (cite); termination, reachability, probabilistic assertions complicate it
  - first logic w/ local reasoning for correctness + incorrectness, can under-approximate paths
  - algebraic representation of choice -> proof extends to other execution models, e.g. probabilistic programs
- Symbolic execution algorithms
  - proof of concept: consolidating correctness + incorrectness analysis; C-like pointer programs
  - core algorithm: all reachable outcomes -> correctness
  - single-path variant modeled after IL bug finders Pulse (cite), Pulse-X (cite); postcondition = one of (possibly many) outcomes
  - scalability of dropping paths; soundly re-use summaries from correctness algorithm, no re-analysis
  - based on bi-abduction: sequential programs, postcondition of one precomputed spec vs precondition of next (cite)
  - effects -> branching (nondeterministic/probabilistic choice) -> tri-abduction, new inference for composing branches
- Outline
  - Sec. 2 challenges of local reasoning in expressive logic
  - Sec. 3, 4 define OSL, three instantiations, frame rule soundness
  - Sec. 5 symbolic execution + tri-abduction (branching, not sequential composition)
  - Sec. 6 two case studies; Sec. 7, 8 outlooks, related work

steps.text:
Static analysis has been scaled to industrial software with hundreds of millions of lines of code by using compositional reasoning with separation logic and bi-abduction. This has made it possible to analyze code changes without disrupting the fast-paced engineering culture that developers are used to.

Fully automated program verification is still an elusive ideal, but analysis tools can increase confidence that code is correct by making sure that a program will not go wrong in a variety of ways. For languages like C or C++, this includes making sure that a program will not crash because of a segmentation fault and will not leak memory. But if a static analyzer fails to prove that there are no bugs, it does not mean that the program is incorrect, it could be a false positive.

In fact many programs are incorrect. So analysis tools that can find bugs are in some cases more useful than verification tools, because the errors they report lead directly to tangible improvements to the code. Incorrectness Logic and Incorrectness Separation Logic (ISL) were introduced recently, and they were motivated by this need to identify bugs.

ISL is compositional just like separation logic, but the semantics of SL and ISL are not compatible, so specifications and analysis tools cannot easily be shared between them. Also, the soundness of local reasoning in each variant of separation logic depends on particular assumptions, and this means that there is no single program logic with a frame rule that can handle all of these:

Computational Effects. The frame rule depends centrally on the idea that program commands must be local actions. To get locality, the semantics of memory allocation is often forced to be nondeterministic, but this does not work for local reasoning in other execution models like probabilistic computation.

May and Must properties. Separation logic can only express properties that must occur, and ISL can only express properties that may occur. A logic for both correctness and incorrectness properties has to handle both may and must properties.

Under-approximation. Bug-finding static analyses are more efficient when they only inspect a subset of the program paths, the ones that lead to a bug. But many separation logics are fault avoiding, which means the precondition must specify the resources needed to execute all traces, so the whole program has to be inspected. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Static analysis has been scaled to industrial software with hundreds of millions of lines of code by using compositional reasoning with separation logic and bi-abduction. This has made it possible to analyze code changes without disrupting the fast-paced engineering culture that developers are used to.

Fully automated program verification is still an elusive ideal, but analysis tools can increase confidence that code is correct by making sure that a program will not go wrong in a variety of ways. For languages like C or C++, this includes making sure that a program will not crash because of a segmentation fault and will not leak memory. But if a static analyzer fails to prove that there are no bugs, it does not mean that the program is incorrect, it could be a false positive.

In fact many programs are incorrect. So analysis tools that can find bugs are in some cases more useful than verification tools, because the errors they report lead directly to tangible improvements to the code. Incorrectness Logic and Incorrectness Separation Logic (ISL) were introduced recently, and they were motivated by this need to identify bugs.

ISL is compositional just like separation logic, but the semantics of SL and ISL are not compatible, so specifications and analysis tools cannot easily be shared between them. Also, the soundness of local reasoning in each variant of separation logic depends on particular assumptions, and this means that there is no single program logic with a frame rule that can handle all of these:

Computational Effects. The frame rule depends centrally on the idea that program commands must be local actions. To get locality, the semantics of memory allocation is often forced to be nondeterministic, but this does not work for local reasoning in other execution models like probabilistic computation.

May and Must properties. Separation logic can only express properties that must occur, and ISL can only express properties that may occur. A logic for both correctness and incorrectness properties has to handle both may and must properties.

Under-approximation. Bug-finding static analyses are more efficient when they only inspect a subset of the program paths, the ones that lead to a bug. But many separation logics are fault avoiding, which means the precondition must specify the resources needed to execute all traces, so the whole program has to be inspected. Fault avoidance does not fit logics for incorrectness.

In this paper we show that local reasoning is sound under new assumptions. These assumptions do not force any particular evaluation model, so they are compatible with both correctness and incorrectness reasoning. For this we introduce Outcome Separation Logic (OSL), a single program logic that handles all of the scenarios above. Our contributions are the following.

Outcome Separation Logic. The main contribution is Outcome Separation Logic (OSL), which extends the recently introduced Outcome Logic (OL) to reason about pointer programs. OL already supports correctness and incorrectness reasoning for programs with a variety of effects, and a lot of the metatheory and inference rules carry over from it. The key new thing in OSL is that it is fundamentally based on heap assertions in the style of separation logic, and this is what let us develop a frame rule for local reasoning and compositional symbolic execution.

This was not easy. The soundness of the frame rule is intricate and nuanced even in partial correctness Hoare Logic, and moving to a logic that supports many kinds of assertions about termination, reachability, and probabilistic reasoning makes it significantly more complicated. OSL is the first program logic that supports local reasoning for both correctness and incorrectness, and it can also under-approximate program paths. In addition, because we use an algebraic representation of choice, the soundness proof of our frame rule also extends to other execution models, such as probabilistic programs.

Symbolic execution algorithms. As a proof of concept of how OSL lets correctness and incorrectness analysis be consolidated, we present symbolic execution algorithms that analyze C-like pointer programs. The core algorithm finds all the reachable outcomes, so it is tailored for correctness reasoning. We also define a single-path variant, modeled after the bug-finding algorithms based on Incorrectness Logic (Pulse and Pulse-X), that infers specifications where the postcondition is only one of the (possibly many) outcomes. It gets the scalability benefit of dropping paths, and our algorithm can also soundly re-use the procedure summaries generated by the correctness algorithm, so the same procedure is not re-analyzed.

The algorithms are based on bi-abduction, which handles sequential programs by reconciling the postcondition of one precomputed spec with the precondition of the next one. Programs with effects are not purely sequential, they have branching that comes from e.g. nondeterministic or probabilistic choice, so we also introduce tri-abduction, a new form of inference for composing branches in an effectful program.

Section 2 outlines the challenges of local reasoning in a highly expressive program logic. In Sections 3 and 4 we define Outcome Separation Logic (OSL), show three instantiations, and prove that the frame rule is sound. In Section 5 we define our symbolic execution algorithm and tri-abduction, which is inspired by bi-abduction but is used for branching instead of sequential composition. Section 6 looks at two case studies to show that these algorithms are applicable, and Sections 7 and 8 conclude with outlooks and related work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Compositional reasoning using separation logic [1] and bi-abduction [2] has helped scale static analysis to industrial software with hundreds of millions of lines of code, making it possible to analyze code changes without disrupting the fast-paced engineering culture developers are used to [3,4].

While fully automated program verification remains an elusive ideal, analysis tools can boost confidence in code correctness by ensuring that a program will not go wrong in a variety of ways. In languages like C or C++, this includes ensuring that a program will not crash due to a segmentation fault or leak memory. However, a static analyzer failing to prove the absence of bugs does not imply that the program is incorrect; it could be a false positive.

Many programs are, in fact, incorrect. Analysis tools that can find bugs are thus in some cases more useful than verification tools, since the errors they report lead directly to tangible code improvements [5]. Motivated by the need to identify bugs, Incorrectness Logic [6] and Incorrectness Separation Logic (ISL) [7,8] were recently introduced.

While ISL is compositional just like separation logic, the semantics of SL and ISL are incompatible—specifications and analysis tools cannot readily be shared between them. Further, the soundness of local reasoning in each separation logic variant relies on particular assumptions, so no single program logic has a frame rule that can handle all of the following:

Computational Effects. The idea that program commands must be local actions [9] is central to the frame rule. To achieve locality, the semantics of memory allocation is often forced to be nondeterministic [10], but this approach is not suitable for local reasoning in alternative execution models such as probabilistic computation.

May and Must properties. Separation logic can only express properties that must occur, whereas ISL can only express properties that may occur. A logic for both correctness and incorrectness properties must handle both may and must properties.

Under-approximation. Bug-finding static analyses operate more efficiently by inspecting only a subset of the program paths—the ones that lead to a bug. But many separation logics are fault avoiding; the precondition must specify the resources needed to execute all traces, so the entire program must be inspected. Fault avoidance is unsuitable in logics for incorrectness.

In this paper, we show that local reasoning is sound under new assumptions, which do not force any particular evaluation model and are therefore compatible with both correctness and incorrectness reasoning. To that end, we introduce Outcome Separation Logic (OSL), a single program logic that can handle all of the scenarios above. Our contributions are as follows.

Outcome Separation Logic. Our main contribution is Outcome Separation Logic (OSL), an extension of the recently introduced Outcome Logic (OL) [11] for reasoning about pointer programs. While OL already supports correctness and incorrectness reasoning in programs with a variety of effects, and much of the metatheory and inference rules carry over from it, the key novelty of OSL is that it is fundamentally based on separation-logic-style heap assertions, which allowed us to develop a frame rule for local reasoning and compositional symbolic execution.

This was not a simple feat; the soundness of the frame rule is intricate and nuanced even in partial correctness Hoare Logic [10], and moving to a logic that supports a variety of assertions about termination, reachability, and probabilistic reasoning complicates the story significantly. OSL is the first program logic that supports local reasoning for both correctness and incorrectness, with the ability to also under-approximate program paths. On top of that, using an algebraic representation of choice, the soundness proof of our frame rule extends to other execution models too, such as probabilistic programs.

Symbolic execution algorithms. As a proof of concept for how OSL enables the consolidation of correctness and incorrectness analysis, we present symbolic execution algorithms to analyze C-like pointer programs. The core algorithm finds all the reachable outcomes, and is therefore tailored for correctness reasoning. We also define a single-path variant—modeled after Incorrectness Logic based bug-finding algorithms (Pulse [7] and Pulse-X [5])—that infers specifications in which the postcondition is just one of the (possibly many) outcomes. While enjoying the scalability benefit of dropping paths, our algorithm can also soundly re-use procedure summaries generated by the correctness algorithm, so the same procedure is not re-analyzed.

These algorithms are based on bi-abduction, which handles sequential programs by reconciling the postcondition of one precomputed spec with the precondition of the next [2,12]. Since programs with effects are not purely sequential but have branching that arises from, e.g., nondeterministic or probabilistic choice, we also introduce tri-abduction, a new form of inference for composing branches in an effectful program.

We begin in Section 2 by outlining the challenges of local reasoning in a highly expressive program logic. In Sections 3 and 4, we define Outcome Separation Logic (OSL), show three instantiations, and prove the soundness of the frame rule. In Section 5, we define our symbolic execution algorithm and tri-abduction, which is inspired by bi-abduction but used for branching rather than sequential composition. In Section 6, we examine two case studies to show the applicability of these algorithms, and we conclude in Sections 7 and 8 by discussing outlooks and related work.
